name: Sara Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a twenty-person firm that specialises in restaurants, cafés and family shops. I do their monthly management accounts, VAT returns and year-end tax, and I've become the person who sets up the AI tools for the rest of the team. A typical morning is me checking what the AI pulled from forty till reports, then fixing the five it got wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love sitting with a café owner and showing them exactly where their profit leaks, usually waste and staff rotas. What wears me out is restaurants that pay us late while asking for more. At home my husband David runs the bakery his grandfather started, so I hear about flour prices at dinner whether I want to or not.

S0.quote: If AI only saves a bit of time, the accountant who saves that time for twenty colleagues becomes the one nobody wants to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a little surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool and nothing more, and the businesses that use it well get a small edge. I'd probably say that in a post for our clients. At church I wouldn't talk about it at all, it's not that kind of place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be in a strong spot. I'm already the one at the firm who makes the tools work, and that makes me useful. If AI only saves a bit of time, the accountant who saves that time for twenty colleagues becomes the one nobody wants to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the AI workflows at the firm and ask the partners to make it part of my role, with a title and a raise. I'd set up the same till-report tool for David's bakery so he stops doing it on Sunday nights. We'd keep our three months of savings and put a bit more towards the bakery's new oven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything already worrying you at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery's margins. Flour and energy went up a lot, and David works six days. My salary is the steady one, so it matters that my job's secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you charge David for the till tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, of course not. He's family. Though I might bring him a bill for fun.

say: I'd call AI a **good tool**, nothing more, giving users a small edge.
I'd write a **client post** about using it well.
think: I'd be in a **strong spot** as the firm's AI person.
My salary is the **steady income** while the bakery's margins are thin.
do: Ask the partners for an **AI role**, title and raise.
Set up a **till-report tool** for David's bakery.
Put a little more towards the bakery's **new oven**.
fieldNote: Sara's **daily AI use** turns a plateau into a career advantage.
Her **husband's bakery** has thin margins, so her salary carries the household.

steps.text: Ask the partners for a formal AI role with a raise
Set up an AI till-report tool for David's bakery
Put a bit more each month towards the bakery's new oven

S1.quote: My colleague Gloria taught me everything when I started, and I'd be the one building the software that makes Gloria's job unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. It's already starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses must adapt or lose to the ones who do, and that's how markets work. I'd tell clients we can do their books faster and cheaper. I wouldn't ask for anyone to protect accountants' jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my firm needs fewer people, and some of my friends there would go. I'd be the one helping to run the tools, so I'd probably stay. But it's strange knowing you're building the thing that replaces your colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the partners to offer cheaper fixed-fee packages to small cafés, run with AI, so we win clients from slower firms. I'd start doing the books for three or four local shops on my own, evenings, for extra income. And I'd learn every new tool as it comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a pang of guilt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria, who's fifty-five and does payroll the old way. My colleague Gloria taught me everything when I started, and I'd be the one building the software that makes Gloria's job unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train her myself, after hours if needed. And I'd tell the partners she's the one clients trust most with bad news.

say: I'd say businesses must **adapt or lose**; that's how markets work.
I'd tell clients we can do their books **faster and cheaper**.
think: The firm needs **fewer people**, though I'd probably stay.
It's strange **building the thing** that replaces my colleagues.
do: Push the partners to sell **AI-run fixed fees** to small cafés.
Do evening **bookkeeping** for three or four local shops.
Train **Gloria** herself so she can keep up.
fieldNote: Sara expects to **keep her job** but watches colleagues at risk.
Her **guilt** about Gloria sits beside free-market views.
Moves first: new pricing, **side clients**, and personal training for a colleague.

steps.text: Pitch AI-run fixed-fee packages to small cafés
Do evening bookkeeping for three or four local shops
Train Gloria on the new payroll tools after hours

S2.quote: I'd rather borrow to grow a family bakery for three good years than sit on three months of savings waiting for the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Two years. Okay, that's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but families and businesses that pull together will get through. I'd tell people at church to lean on each other rather than wait for the government. Online I'd share what's working for small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job wouldn't survive it. Knowing the tools is worth nothing when the tools don't need me. The bakery is hands-on, so it has about three years more, until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the bakery within the first year and run the business side: ordering, pricing, the online shop. I'd use AI for all of that so David can bake more. We'd use our savings and a small loan to open a second shop while there's still time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a loan risky right when your salary disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is risky. I'd rather borrow to grow a family bakery for three good years than sit on three months of savings waiting for the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the bakery when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe people still want bread from a family they know. Maybe they don't, and we'd have to sell.

say: I'd say families and businesses that **pull together** will get through.
I'd tell church friends to **lean on each other**, not wait for government.
think: The **bakery** has about three more years, until 2031.
Knowing the tools is **worth nothing** once they don't need me.
do: Move into the **bakery's business side** within the first year.
Use AI for **ordering and pricing** so David bakes more.
Open a **second shop** with savings and a small loan.
fieldNote: Sara expects to **lose her accounting job** but takes a risky step anyway.
Her plan rests on the **robot gap** for hands-on baking.
She admits **not knowing** what happens to the bakery after 2031.

steps.text: Leave the firm to run the bakery's ordering and pricing
Use AI tools for the bakery's orders and online shop
Open a second bakery shop with savings and a small loan

S3.quote: Five years' warning means I can open the second bakery with our own money instead of the bank's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to do this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a real opportunity for anyone willing to work. At church and with clients I'd encourage family businesses to modernise now. I'd write about it for our client newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at the firm for two or three years, earning while I build up the bakery on the side. By 2031 my accounting job goes, but the bakery has until about 2034. I think we'd come out of it fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the bakery's books and online orders evenings and weekends with AI tools. I'd save my salary hard for two years and then open the second shop in 2029. Around 2030 I'd leave the firm and join David full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit uneasy about leaving the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until 2029 for the second shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want the savings to pay for it, not a loan. Five years' warning means I can open the second bakery with our own money instead of the bank's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents think of this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad thinks I'm mad to leave a professional job for a bakery. But he also built his own business, so he'll come round.

say: I'd call it a real **opportunity** for anyone willing to work.
I'd urge family businesses to **modernise now**.
think: I'd **stay at the firm** two or three years while building the bakery.
The bakery lasts until about **2034**, after my job ends.
do: Run the bakery's **books and online orders** evenings with AI.
**Save her salary** hard for two years.
Open the **second shop** in 2029 and join David full time by 2030.
fieldNote: Five years lets Sara fund growth **without debt**.
She expects her **household income** to hold through the bakery.
Her **father's doubts** are the main friction she mentions.

steps.text: Run the bakery's books and online orders on weekends
Save most of her salary for two years
Open a second bakery shop in 2029 with savings
Leave the firm in 2030 to join David full time

S4.quote: By 2039 our bakery will either be a local name people choose on purpose, or it won't, and ten years is long enough to make it the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say anyone who plans has plenty of time. I'd tell clients to use the decade to strengthen their businesses. I'd be firmly against big handouts that stop people adjusting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it suits us. I'd have most of a decade as an accountant, a growing bakery, and time for children. By 2036 I'd be out of accounting anyway and in our own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the firm and lead its AI work for the next few years. We'd open a second bakery around 2030 and maybe a third later. We'd also start a family in the next two or three years, which we'd been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Genuinely calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2039. Does that worry you for the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. By 2039 our bakery will either be a local name people choose on purpose, or it won't, and ten years is long enough to make it the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If David's health went, or if the bakery lost money two years running. Then I'd stay in accounting longer and rethink.

say: I'd say anyone who plans has **plenty of time**.
I'd oppose **big handouts** that stop people adjusting.
I'd tell clients to use the decade to **strengthen** their businesses.
think: The decade **suits us**: accounting income, a growing bakery, time for children.
By 2036 I'd be in **our own business** anyway.
do: Keep leading the firm's **AI work** for several years.
Start a **family** within two or three years.
fieldNote: With ten years Sara sees the change as **good for her household**.
Her backup **triggers** are David's health or two losing years.
**Family plans** come forward because the timeline feels safe.

steps.text: Keep leading the firm's AI work for several years
Open a second bakery shop around 2030
Start a family within two or three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd be borrowing against a bakery with a clock on it. What would help is easier small-business lending and lower taxes on family firms, so people can build something instead of waiting for a cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how this changes marriages. My husband bakes bread with his hands at four in the morning, and I never thought his job would be the safer one in our house.

headlineQuote: My husband bakes bread with his hands at four in the morning, and I never thought his job would be the safer one in our house.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old accountant** at a firm serving restaurants, cafés and family shops.
She uses **AI daily** and is the firm's go-to for setting up the tools.
She's married to David, who runs his grandfather's **bakery** on thin margins.
She holds **free-market**, faith-based views but feels **guilt** about colleagues at risk.
In every AGI picture she moves into **the bakery**, timing it to the robot gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, borrowing against a **bakery** with a clock on it.
whatWouldHelp: Easier **small-business lending** and **lower taxes** on family firms.
